newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian retail reverses poor Christmas in Q1.
newsitem.headline: Australian retail reverses poor Christmas in Q1.

text.p: Australia's retail sector turned around a disappointing Christmas period in the first quarter of 1997, with official data released on Friday showing it will make a strong contribution to first quarter economic growth.
Retail trade actually dipped 0.3 percent in March, but that was still a sign of strength given it followed rises of 0.8 and 2.7 percent in February and January respectively.
In real terms, retail trade rose 2.2 percent over the March quarter, more than reversing December's 1.3 percent fall.

"It looks safe to say that the worst is behind the retail sector, even though it is likely to be three to six months before there is a fully fledged upswing," Citibank Australia chief economist Stephen Koukoulas said.
While the monthly dip was slightly below expectations of a flat result, the quarterly rise implied a strong contribution to first quarter gross domestic product (GDP), which is due in early June.
"No reason for concern even though there is a modest fall of 0.3 percent," GIO Australia chief economist Akis Haralabopoulos said.
"The important thing to focus on in the retail trade figures is the quarterly numbers showing a 2.2 percent increase."
Economists put the retail contribution at around 0.5 percentage points to expenditure based GDP.
Given strength in March quarter vehicle sales, and expected continuation of spending on services, private sector consumption should be one of the strongest areas of first quarter growth.

Along with the housing sector, the strength in retail trade in early 1997 has been one of the key factors behind expectations of stronger economic growth later this year, and an argument against the need for further interest rate cuts to
follow the three made last year.

"The interest rate cuts of 1996 appear to be having their desired impact on the interest rate sensitive sectors such as consumption, and should continue to assist this sector as the year progresses," Hambros fixed income economist Su-Lin Ong said.
However, like other areas of the economy in recovery, the pace of improvement is expected to be more gradual in previous upswings, given the economy remains patchy.
"One constraint to the expected recovery in the retail sector could be the weakness in the labour market, from both an income and confidence effect," Citibank's Koukoulas said.

As well, some felt the strength in the quarter was attributable to a shift in consumer spending to the post-Christmas sales period and ongoing discounting by retailers, which may have overstated the underlying pace of spending.

"Retail trade figures next month then will most probably suggest that the pick up in retail trade witnessed in the first part of this year lasted a little over one month and moderated around Febrtuary/March," Societe Generale economist Glenn Maguire said.
With that sort of outlook, there was also no pressing need for an increase in rates.
While the near term risk was for a rate cut, especially if employment remained weak, economists said the most likely scenario was a period of steady official rates.

"We remain of the view that monetary policy is on hold -- and contine to see the probabilities favouring the next move being a tightening in the first half of 1998," HSBC Markets chief economist John Edwards said.
